explanation: This pole fires on structural punctuation inside a formal constructed expression: commas separating listed items (function arguments, array dimensions, SQL column lists), opening brackets starting argument or index lists, dots joining dotted attribute chains, and terminal marks closing markup-embedded phrases. The same characters in plain prose stay silent: commas after 'Paris' or '1969' and sentence-final dots score 0, a semicolon substituted into a code-comma slot scores 0, and the identical 'Hello, world!' string fires only inside its HTML frame.

This pole is a retrospective detector for the aspirated-b consonant pair 'bh' (a 'b'/'B' immediately followed by 'h') in rare, non-native words. It peaks at the sub-word token carrying the 'h': the pair may straddle a token boundary ('Ab'|'hay' 15.2, 'V'|'ib'|'hu' 8.9, 'b'|'hang' 8.9, 'B'|'hop' 7.6, Hindi भारत 'bhārat' 9.9) or sit inside one ('ĠBh' fires at the identical 3.56 in Bhutan, Bhishma, Bhakti and Bhavan); it also fires one step weaker (1-8) on the h-bearing word-internal fragment of other rare or foreign words (Bischoffsgemälde 'cho' 7.9, Brihadaranyaka 'had' 4.8, Hsiang 'ang' 4.2, Verhängen 'äng' 3.4), while every other consonant+h pair is an order of magnitude weaker (gh 1.3, vh 1.7, kh 0.5, ch/dh/sh/th/ph/wh/zh < 0.1), a fragment without 'h' stays near zero, and the strength is fixed by the left context (changing the words after the peak leaves the value bit-identical).

This pole is a retrospective detector for a 'Tro'/'tro' word onset at the current position: it fires on whole tokens spelling Tro-words ('Troy', 'Trojan', 'troll', 'trolling'), on subword onset pieces (' tro', ' Tro', ' Tr', ' T'/'t', Cyrillic ' тр', Greek ' τρ') and on their within-word continuations ('roy', 'j', 'rolling', 'ans'), but not on the same continuations without the onset ('rolling', 'Roy', 'toll') nor on other tr-initial or mid-word -tr- tokens ('truck', 'traffic', 'treat', 'control', 'street'). Its gain is set by the immediate left context, strongest after determiners/prepositions ('the', 'to', 'of', 'from') and weakest after verbs like 'say'/'found', but the onset-trigger requirement itself is strict.

This pole is a retrospective detector of the word 'tradition' — the lexeme, not the idea it names: it fires at the token that spells or carries the word, peaking on a subword piece of a split spelling (the 'и' of 'традиции', the '統' of '伝統', the '통' of '전통'), on English tradition/traditions/traditional/traditionally and on the bare ' trad' subword wherever the tokenizer splits it out (tradere, traduce, traduire, traduction, traducción, traduzione, tradimento), on the trad- loanwords of the European languages (tradición, tradizione, tradições, traditie, tradities, tradice, tradicija, tradycja, Tradition/tradition, традиция/традиції/традиција, ტრადიცია), on the Sinitic 傳統/传统/伝統/전통 (the final 統/统/통 read after 傳/传/伝/전) and on the Arabic التقاليد/تقليد. Words for the same idea with a different root (custom(s), heritage, ritual, convention, customary, 习俗/习惯/관습, обычаи, عادة, تراث, costumbre, coutume, Brauch, Sitte, παράδοση, परंपरा, gelenek) stay below the active line, as do single-token trad- lookalikes (trade, trader, trademark, trading, tragedy, trajectory, translation, extradition); a single-token spelling at the text's very first position ('Traditional medicine…', '传统…') also stays below the line, because the pole's gain needs a preceding token.

The negative pole fires on the penal outcome of a criminal case: the punishment a court imposes or carries out on a person and the guilt it rests on. Its strongest triggers are penalty phrases - 'sentenced/imposed/condemned to' a term ('life', 'death', 'twelve years', 'eleven months', prison, probation), 'life sentence', 'death sentence', 'death penalty', 'capital punishment', parole, the execution or lethal injection of a condemned prisoner, and the reduction or appeal of a penalty ('reduced/lessened/commuted/vacated a sentence') - together with the guilt finding ('pleaded guilty', 'plea of guilty', 'guilty verdict', 'verdict was guilty', a conviction being appealed, 'guilt', and graded serious charges such as 'first degree', 'capital', 'aggravated'). Because the trigger is the penal phrase, the same words with no penal left context ('The sentence was announced', 'Executions are carried out at dawn') stay near zero, and strength grows as several cues accumulate. It is the complement of the positive pole, which fires when the authorities take a person into restraint (arrest, custody, detention, jail, apprehension - all near zero here), and it stays near zero on crimes named without a penalty (murder, rape, fraud, burglary), on investigation and charging procedure (indictment, arraignment, prosecution, testimony, jury instructions), on civil litigation and money remedies (contract, damages, negligence, fines, restitution), and on the everyday senses of the same words ('sentence' of a paragraph, 'execution' of a plan or contract, 'life' in the ocean, 'death' of a patient, 'degree' in mathematics); a few court-room words from the legal documents it fires in ('public defender', 'defense attorney', 'assistance of counsel', 'vacate', 'handed down') reach only the low active range. Its output direction promotes this same penal lexicon rather than a specific next token, so the mechanism is retrospective.

The positive pole is a retrospective detector for the linking ' of' and/or the head token of a stock two-noun 'X of Y' compound term in its bare form (no determiner after 'of'): it fires strongest on quality of life (peaks 10-13 at both ' of' and ' Life'), then end of life, bill of materials, terms of service, quality of service, cost of living, depth of field and field of vision (4-10 at the peak), and quality of care and point of view (3-6), while the words alone are inert (' service' reads 0.6 alone but 8.5 in 'terms of service'). Membership is lexical, not semantic or frequency-driven: substituting a merely similar domain noun keeps only the weak ' of' response (quality of education 1.6-3.8 vs 10.4), and compositional of-phrases of other shapes stay at the floor (place of birth 0.1-0.9, state of the art 0.2-0.7, speed of light 0.3-0.6, cause of death 1.3-2.4); reordering ('life quality', 'service terms') kills the peak, a determiner after 'of' roughly halves it (quality of the life 4.0 vs 10.4), the hyphenated/glued spellings are the same feature and fire as strongly or stronger (quality-of-life 13.5, ease-of-development 10.0, time-of-flight 7.6, out-of-the-box 6.4, internetofthings 3.5), and arbitrary initialisms mostly stay at the floor (only the scanned stored strings fire: SIL OFL, R.O.C., BOD, BioFOG, nOTScale, POV).

The pole is a gastroenterology feature: it fires when the current token carries clinical content of the gastrointestinal tract and abdominal cavity in medical prose — bowel/intestine/colonic/rectal/peritoneal/retroperitoneal/abdominal/biliary anatomy, GI procedures and investigations (stent, colonoscopy, colectomy, ileostomy, biopsies, stricture, abdominal imaging) and GI pathology (diverticulitis, malabsorption, polyps, diarrhoea, abdominal cramping). Everyday health words, other organ systems (kidney, liver, heart, lung function), lay non-GI symptom talk and non-medical technical jargon leave it near zero, with only a weak (~0.2 of peak) tail on other specialist clinical terms such as imaging or device vocabulary; its negative pole is the complementary stomach/acid-reflux complaint cluster (heartburn, reflux, peptic ulcer), whose tokens the positive pole's output suppresses.

This pole fires on colloquial, online/spoken-register English: internet-slang and meme vocabulary (derp, snark, facepalm, noob, epic fail, meme, shitpost, lol, ugh, meh, lowkey, cringe, dope), internet-culture names (xkcd, Tumblr, 4chan, Homestuck, Boing Boing, Pastafarian, Rainbow Dash) and conversational fillers and hedges (basically, kinda, pretty much, literally, thing, such, whatever, just), while it is near-silent on formal edited prose and on ordinary standard words of similar meaning (bad, rough, cool, party, event, Facebook, embarrassing), so swapping a slang word for its formal synonym is predicted to switch it off. Its peaks land mid-word on the register-carrying word itself (e.g. 'ark' in snark) with nothing unusual following, and its output weights promote the same register (shit, fuck, badass, -ish, bullshit, derp, Tumblr), so it is a style detector, not a next-token predictor.

The pole is a term detector for search-engine marketing: it fires on the vocabulary webmasters and search advertisers use about a page's standing in web search - 'SEO', 'Yoast', 'search engine(s)', 'keywords', 'Pay Per Click'/'PPC', 'rank'/'ranking', 'optimise'/'optimisation'/'optimised', 'backlinks', 'SERP', 'sitemap', 'noindex', 'Googlebot', 'meta description', 'domain authority', 'Search Console', 'webmaster tools', and 'Google'/'Yahoo' named as search engines (also the equivalents in other languages, e.g. 排名/优化, 搜索引擎, posicionamiento en buscadores) - plus, more weakly, the page-head markup that carries search metadata ('meta description', 'meta robots'/'noindex', 'link rel=canonical' or 'hreflang'), and it is strongest when several such terms co-occur in one passage. The same words in other senses (a matrix's or an officer's 'rank', a missing 'link', a 'meta'-analysis, supply-chain 'optimisation', Google's corporate news), non-search advertising (television, print, email, social), generic web words ('website', 'page', 'hosting', 'stylesheet', 'browser', a plain https URL) and SEO advice reworded without these terms ('climb the results page', 'earn citations') do not fire: the trigger is the search-marketing term itself, not the general idea.

Predicted active: the head token of a noun phrase that names a mathematical result or statement (theorem, lemma, inequality, principle, law, test, limit, formula) used as a term of art, with activity building over the words that lead into the term and peaking on that head (e.g. 'theorem' in 'the mean value theorem' ~16, 'numbers' in 'the law of large numbers' ~15, 'test' in 'the ratio test' ~8, 'inequality' in 'the triangle inequality' ~6), and usually falling back to the noise floor on the next word. Predicted inactive: ordinary prose, non-mathematical senses of the same words ('the law was passed', 'social inequality', 'she passed the test easily', all <=0.6), and mathematical objects that are not result words ('function', 'matrix', 'equation', 'transform'), which stay at the 0.1-0.4 noise floor.

Retrospective detector that fires when the current token asserts a binary pairing, mirror-image, equivalence, or opposition relation between two items or claims (opposite ends/sides, counterparts, equivalents, mirror/mirroring, duality-double as in double-stranded/double-edged, or discourse inversion such as conversely, vice versa, on the contrary); quantity senses of double and other non-relational words stay near floor.

Retrospective: the negative pole fires on tokens inside a reference to content that is hosted and shared on the web - the host, path or query of a share link (jsfiddle.net, codepen.io, pastebin.com, stackblitz, codesandbox, replit, imgur, youtube.../watch?v=) - and, more weakly, on the publishing vocabulary of such web posts and Q&A/video pages (video/videos, channel, upload, views, answers, questions, Q&A, edit mode). Ordinary prose, URLs with no share target (example.org/page), generic software or reference-site names (kubernetes, webpack, github, wikipedia) and the same words in their everyday offline senses stay inactive.

The pole fires on clauses that assert the existence, presence, location, containment, composition or possession of a concrete physical thing (as opposed to a plan, report, argument or idea) - the stative 'be-at / have' relation: presentational 'there is/are X (in Y)', 'X is located/situated/stands/lies/lives/grows/inhabits Y', 'X is home to Y', 'X contains/includes/holds/houses/comprises/consists of/is made up of Y', 'X has Y', and extent or name statements about such a thing ('X is 200 kilometres long', 'X is called/known as Y'); it peaks on the relation word, or on the clause-final copula/existential in languages that mark the predicate there (Hindi है/हैं, Japanese です/である/にある/あります, Korean 있다, Russian было/расположена/находится). It does not fire on eventive predicates and their passives (X was built/founded/destroyed/sold/found, X burned/fell/moved/grew), on one-place quality adjectives ('the rock is heavy', 'the sky is blue'), or on non-spatial and abstract-discourse relations ('the letter was written by the author', 'the plan has three stages', 'the report includes a summary').

The pole fires on the abstract concept of reinforcement — a reward, punishment or other incentive whose function is to drive or shape behaviour, in any register — rather than on the goods involved or on the word forms. It peaks on reinforcement vocabulary and frames (reward, incentive, reinforcement, motivate/motivation, encourage/discourage/deter, reward and loyalty programmes, the carrot-and-stick idiom, operant conditioning) and on the brain's reward circuitry (dopamine, nucleus accumbens, mesocorticolimbic, ventral tegmental), while payment and bounty senses (a cash reward for information, salary, bonus, prize, gift) and metaphorical or evaluative uses of the same stems (a rewarding experience, encouraging results) stay near baseline.

This pole fires on astrobiology and planetary-science text - passages about water, ice, oceans, atmospheres, habitable conditions, or the search for life and biosignatures on other worlds - and it peaks on the token that carries that content (' water', ' ice', ' ocean', ' life', ' habitable', ' rivers'). The same words in everyday, terrestrial, molecular-biology, engineering or political contexts leave it near zero (measured peaks: 'On Mars, scientists found water' = 13.9 vs 'In Peru, scientists found water' = 1.2, 'The enzyme catalyses...' = 0.3), though a bare science-discovery sentence about water ('Scientists found water.') still gives a partial response (~10).

Fires on tokens that belong to standardised wording about permission, verification or practice rather than to composed prose: licence and legal-notice formulas ('Licensed under the ... License', 'WITHOUT WARRANTIES OR CONDITIONS OF ANY KIND', an 'AS IS' BASIS), code and markup boilerplate (annotation lines above 'public void setUp()', MODULE_LICENSE, '.flags =' field rows, '/test' path segments, layout_constraint attributes, CSS px values), and established care/testing/rehearsal phrasing ('memtest', 'chmod 644 ... permissions', 'buff with a clean cloth', 'practiced/trained/rehearsed for months'). Ordinary narrative prose, famous quotations, generic numbered steps and the same key words in plain sentences ('the license permits redistribution', 'without any warranty', 'the test suite', 'she worked for years') leave it at zero.

This pole fires retrospectively on passages describing a formally attested collective procedure: a population being surveyed or sampled (surveyed N citizens, a survey conducted among randomly selected members), a choice being elected or voted on by members, or a protocol, decision, or message being approved or signed by a committee or key. Removing the attestation verb while keeping the numbers and group nouns collapses activity; edits outside such procedures do nothing.

The pole fires on the tokens by which a passage marks the participants or the outcome of a sports competition: a team's, club's or school's name or nickname ('North Carolina', 'Duke', 'Real Madrid', 'the Yankees', 'Boilermakers'), the fixed side designators 'home/away/visiting team' and 'home/away side', two team names coordinated as a subject ('Duke and Yale', 'Michigan State and Purdue'), a field of entries ('athletes from 23 countries', '23 National Olympic Committees'), and a game's score line ('89 – 72'). It is silent when the same place, institution, person or company names are not read as competitors ('I grew up in Michigan', 'He studied at Duke and Yale', 'Madrid and Barcelona are cities'), and on named individual athletes ('Nadal beat Federer'), generic 'team' ('the team bus', 'the basketball team') and sports words that name no participant or result ('the tournament was cancelled', 'the Olympic Games').

The pole fires on general, normative claims about the accountability and integrity of public institutions, the officials who run them, and the systems the public relies on: statements that power is abused or corrupted, that agencies, officials or elections are unaccountable, untrustworthy or open to interference, or that oversight, transparency and safeguards are needed against such abuse or human error. The same vocabulary inside a report of a specific incident (who resigned, was charged or jailed on which day) or in ordinary politics (campaigns, budgets, votes) leaves it near baseline.

Fires on a noun phrase that designates a specific made product or work by its make - a brand, manufacturer, model or creator name attached to, or standing in for, the product - as in 'Joey Calderazzo's composition', 'the first Harrison composition', 'a Smith tune', 'the Sony F900', 'the HTC Hero', 'a Gillette Silver Blue blade', 'two Sonys', 'My Sony', 'the Plymouth Hemi 'Cuda'; the peak lands within that make+product designation, on the make name itself (Sony, Plymouth, HTC) or on the product or work noun that completes it (composition, recording), and is strongest when the designation is the new-information object or complement of the clause (after 'closes with', 'opens with', 'bought', 'owns'). It is near zero for the same name in its company sense ('Sony announced...', 'made by Sony', 'from Sony'), for the same product or work noun with no make or only an ordinary adjective ('a simple composition', 'a short tune', 'I bought a camera'), for a clause-subject use of the same phrase ('The Smith composition was well received'), and for a make name modifying a non-product noun ('a Smith house').

Retrospective detector of a discourse pivot: the pole fires on a contrast/update marker (but, however, sentence-initial Now/Next, or a but/how/what/why question) only when the preceding context establishes a success, expectation, concession, or completed background item and the peak introduces its limitation, exception, unresolved remainder, or next development. The same surface tokens without that two-part setup (plain 'and'-coordination, intra-clause 'but', adverbial 'right now', or a question asked without prior concession) stay quiet.

Retrospective detector for the token that completes or punctuates a conventional formal-reference chunk (a field-separator comma in an affiliation, address, or bibliographic line; the second half of a frozen legal or academic collocation such as license to reproduce, notify users, legitimate interests, studies in advanced mathematics, or Law Number 10 of 1998; or a Latin, taxonomic, abbreviation, statute, or measurement completion such as pl., U.S.C., or citation digits), active only when the surrounding passage is a formal reference, license or terms clause, citation, or address block. The same tokens in ordinary prose, isolated commas without the formal frame, or formal words with the conventional chunk broken stay low.

This pole detects search/listing result-count displays: text that reports how many items a search, listing or pagination produced — pagination and summary lines ('Showing 1 - 20 of 350 results', 'Search results: 1 - 10 of 55', 'Displaying 20 of 350 results', 'Results 1 - 1 of 1', 'Page 1 of 35') and result-count sentences ('Found 350 matching results', 'The search found 123 results', 'Showing 25 results per page'). It peaks on the numerals and the adjacent function/count words (' -', ' of', ' results', digits) inside such a frame, while numerals in ordinary narrative prose ('The experiment produced 123 results', 'There were 350 people at the event') and bare labeled numbers ('Order number 12345', 'Price: $1,234') stay inactive; page-view/session counters (e.g. 'has viewed by 51 users', 'based on 27 sessions') fire when a page-template context supports them but are weak and unreliable in isolation.

The pole fires when the preceding text marks a place, record, field, list, role or status as unfilled or unsettled: explicitly absent or empty (blank, empty, vacant, missing, unfilled, no entry, no content, None/placeholder, unemployed, derelict), unknown or unresolved (unknown, unclear, uncertain, undecided, inconclusive, unanswered, unsolved, doubt, up in the air, on hold), or only temporary or provisional (temporary, interim, for a time, sabbatical, leave of absence). It is retrospective and semantic rather than lexical, and it does not fire on positive-polarity synonyms of the same state (open, available, free), on ordinary event negation (did not buy), on hedges or vague quantities (about, perhaps, a few), on plain durations (the entire summer), on containers holding a physical substance (the bottle was empty) or on settled negative states (closed, dead, lost, failed).

The pole fires where a sentence specifies the physical properties of a concrete object: an attributive size, dimension, material or colour word on the noun ('wider aisles and a larger produce department', 'high ceilings, wide windows', 'a 14-inch display', 'made of dark wood'), or an explicit measure ('thirty centimetres across', 'two metres long', 'a fine pitch of a metal wiring'), with the peak usually landing on the function word that follows the modified noun phrase. It does not fire when the same objects are merely mentioned bare ('the aisles and the produce department'), nor on narrative action, abstract political or economic argument, or a bare date or count.

This pole fires on or just after a subordinating or relational marker (after, due to, if, when, upon, as, arrival of, replaced) when the preceding passage frames someone filling, inheriting, joining, or being selected for a role, spot, or individualized outcome, typically because another party is absent, injured, dead, withdrawn, disqualified, or displaced. The same markers stay near zero in neutral temporal, celebratory, weather, or routine passages with no substitution-or-selection frame, and the peak is driven by the preceding frame rather than the words that follow it.

The negative pole fires on the token that closes a slot in laid-out text - the ':' ending an aligned 'Label:' field, the final character of a padded identifier, citation, docket number or filename, the tail of a Markdown underline or ASCII rule, a table cell, or a sentence-final period before a wide gap - i.e. on the token immediately before a whitespace-only token (padding spaces or a blank line), with the peak on that closing token rather than on the whitespace. It requires the layout to be established earlier in the document: the same words with single spaces between fields stay near baseline (0.44 of 11.56), a lone padded line reaches only 0.09, and one earlier padded line lifts the next field's ':' from 0.09 to 4.53; its output direction promotes exactly those padding whitespace tokens, but the zero-ablation KL averaged over the base prompts is 3.1e-4, below the lookahead threshold, because the pole is active on fewer than 0.1% of scan tokens, so the mechanism is claimed retrospective.

The negative pole fires where a text is enumerating or paralleling things: at the punctuation that ends one member of a series and lets the next begin — a comma, semicolon, colon or line break between members ('A, B, and C', a label followed by its description, 'one ... and the other ...', 'the first is ... and the second is ...', 'divided into five age groups: 1-4 years, 5-9 years, ...') — or at the period that closes one member's description in an announced set ('there are two types ...; the first are ...'). It is weak in ordinary narrative, argumentative and expository prose with no series in progress (clause commas, relative clauses, sentence-final periods) and in a bare list of one-word items that no sentence announces; its write direction nudges continuation and alternative markers ('also', 'or', 'and', 'etc', 'instead', 'rather') rather than any specific next token.

The pole fires on the count/numeral token that states how much a thing actually contains or has, when an earlier clause in the same sentence has just given that thing's apparent, claimed or expected amount ("the bag looks like a single portion but really contains two portions"; "the sign says one lane, but the road actually has two lanes."), the peak landing on the actual-amount count. Neither half alone fires it: a bare count ("the bag contains two portions"), a bare appearance claim ("the bag looks like a single portion") and a plain quantifier ("all of the students") all stay inactive, so the cue is the apparent-versus-actual amount contrast rather than the token or the noun.

The pole fires on prefabricated rather than composed wording: the terse credit/apparatus formats that name a document's source — a byline ('By <name>', or a name alone on its line above the agency/role, e.g. 'Maria Sanchez' over 'Bloomberg News'), a photo credit ('<name>/<agency>', 'via AP'), a citation's '<surname>, ed.', and the head of a 'References'/'External links'/'Category:' block — and, at similar strength, conventional clause templates in running prose, above all a relative clause whose subject is focused by 'only' with a modal predicate ('the kind of view that only a grandmother can cook up', 'the road that only buses can use') and a clause-final elliptical modal ('like a proper movie should'). It falls to the floor (under 10% of max) when the same information is composed as an ordinary sentence ('Maria Sanchez of Bloomberg News wrote about the warning', 'Jane Doe took the photos for Reuters', 'which T H Grengy edited', 'external files'), when the template's 'only' becomes 'any' or its modal is dropped, and in plain narrative prose; the negative pole instead fires on the specific named agent a claim is sourced to ('analysts', 'Reuters'), not on the generic role nouns a composed sentence uses ('the staff', 'the news agency').

The pole fires at the token where a sentence commits to a proposition it presents as information: the copula or evidential predicate after an abstract claim/information subject (“the fact/truth/reality/claim/rumour/hypothesis/assumption/premise/implication/bottom line/point/reason/conclusion/result/situation is/was/remains”, and “the news/evidence/report/statement/view/opinion is that …”, where the peak lands on the complementizer “that”), or the reporting/evidential verb whose subject is an information source (“the report/newspaper/magazine/press/study/research/data/figures/polls/survey/census/memo/rules/law/contract/court/government reports/reported/states/says/shows/reveals/indicates/suggests/concludes/claims/notes/adds/confirms/announced/found/ruled”). It is retrospective — the peak is fixed once its prefix is read and no continuation changes it — and it stays quiet on direct predication about concrete objects, events or physical properties (“the car is red”, “the report was long and boring”, “the ministry is closed on Monday”), on personal or first-person opinion verbs (“I think”, “the girl says that …”, “the witness reported that …”), and on non-assertive uses of the same words (“he reports to the manager”, “the bell indicates the end of class”).

L19/N4805- (negative pole) is a retrospective detector of a comparative/associative relation attached to a determiner + singular concrete noun: it spikes on the relator token that directly follows such a noun phrase, most strongly on the bare preposition 'like' ('a wheel like a star' 7.4, 'a window like a star' 6.0, 'a bottle/cup/box like ...' 4.1-4.8, and the scan's top example 'a ball of light like “a flying star with a fiery tail”' at 6.6) and more weakly on 'related' after a noun phrase ('technologies related to the treatment of water' 1.1-3.7). It stays at baseline when 'like' is verbal or part of a verbal collocation ('I like ...', 'looks like ...'), when a comma, an adjective or a relative clause intervenes ('a window, like ...', 'a big window like ...', 'that looks like ...'), when another relator is used instead ('near', 'unlike', 'similar to', 'connected to', 'relevant to'), and when the head noun is mass or abstract ('a smell like ...', 'a water like ...', 'music like ...'); the weaker firings on code-format tokens (Javadoc ' *', '>', '//') and on broken/foreign byte fragments ('�', Devanagari mojibake) are acknowledged leftovers this audit does not explain.

Fires retrospectively on a report's citing span: it peaks on the pivot that introduces a named outside source ('was obtained/reported/confirmed ... by/to X', 'on <site>', 'a review on X', 'an interview with X', 'appeared previously on X', 'source: X', and 'told/tells X' where X is a named outlet and the speaker is a designated source such as a spokesperson or named official) and on the source's own name tokens (a publication, website or outlet name, URL/domain pieces such as '://', or a byline bracket such as '【'). The pivot's firing is set by the preceding text alone, so the object it introduces does not change it; the pole stays inactive on non-citing passives ('was reviewed/written by'), on a bare publication name with no citing role, on an outlet used only as the subject of a reporting verb ('Al Jazeera reported ...'), and on ordinary locative phrases ('on the kitchen table').

Fires on the word 'single' itself (any case, including the subword 'ingle' in camelCase 'singleLine') when it is used in its plain counting/category sense of 'exactly one unit' or 'one-unit kind' (single-photon, single-center, a single game, single room/ticket, single mother, 'I am single'), at roughly 0.6-1.0 of max; other multiplicity words fire much more weakly (double ~0.35-0.45, multi/dual/sole/mon(o)/one ~0.1-0.3, return/twin/great ~0). The pole is strongly suppressed (<~0.25 of max) when 'single' is the emphatic polarity intensifier after 'every', 'not a', 'not one', 'without a' or 'just a', or the music-release noun after 'released', 'new', 'latest', 'first' or 'lead'; plain predicate negation ('I am not single') does not suppress it, and tokens after 'single' are inactive.

The pole fires when a passage puts an abstract object or concept into words: the peak lands on the verb, adverb or qualifier that carries a statement, definition, description or expression ('stated', 'defined', 'described', 'expressed', 'characterised', 'formulated', 'formally', 'explicitly'), most strongly in a passive or definitional frame about an abstract subject ('this problem can be stated as follows', 'the syntax can be formally defined', 'the theorem can be described in one sentence'), and more weakly on technical attributive qualifiers inside abstract noun phrases ('initial', 'statistical', 'typical-set'). It stays near zero on narrative action, concrete everyday predications, instructions, code, and on non-verbal predicates of the same shape ('can be measured', 'can be represented', 'can be painted').

This pole fires retrospectively when the text read so far frames an adverse outcome, hazard, defect, or risk — bodily injury or illness, safety violations, product defects, violence or infringement, errors and faults, or content warnings — with activation building over the framing phrase and typically peaking on the token just before the word that names the harm. Concern-laden nouns such as liver or wrinkles drive it only inside a worry or medical-harm framing, not in neutral uses (liver and onions, wrinkles in fabric), and its output direction promotes bilingual risk and harm vocabulary (risk, worries, concerns,隐患,风险) while suppressing positive-achievement tokens.

The positive pole fires on text that reports a statistical result or an epidemiological quantity: it peaks inside hypothesis-test and effect-size notation ('P<0.001', 'p = 0.03', 'OR = 1.34; 95% CI 1.10-1.63', 'SE 0.08', '80% power', '± 8.1') and on the measures such results are stated in (incidence, prevalence, cohort, lesion, morbidity, mortality), taking its peak on the digit or punctuation that completes the notation (the '.' of '0.001', the ';' after 'OR = 1.34'); a clinical value recorded for a patient ('temperature 38.5 C', 'blood pressure 140/90') is a weaker trigger of the same kind. It is a statistics detector rather than a citation- or medical-topic-register detector: 'Smith et al., 2020', '[1],[2]', Table/Figure references, qualitative-methods prose, narrative clinical text, non-statistical numbers in everyday prose (recipes, prices, bridge spans, sports scores) and 'clinical practice' prose all stay inactive, with adjacent LaTeX citation markup ('[@ref1],[@ref2]', peak about 3.6, half the statistical peaks) the one non-statistical trigger found, while the 'clinical practice' clause drives the negative pole instead (strength 19.7 on ' clinical'), so one sentence can be strongly positive on its p-value and strongly negative on its 'clinical practice' clause.

The pole fires on the digit tokens of a date reference to a year in 1000-1999: it peaks on the '9' of a 1900s year ('in 1989', 'of 1964', 'Oct. 15, 1903', '(1928-2014)', 'the 1920s', 'the 19th century'), fires less strongly on the '1' that opens any such year, and stays near zero for 2000s years ('In 2019'), for the same digits used as a bare count or label ('19 people', '1932 seats', 'Room 1932'), and for '19' inside a longer numeral. Its strength tracks how strongly the passage reads as a dated factual chronicle - the same year fires about 4 in a neutral sentence but about 18 after a natural-hazard or disruption statement ('Solar storms can damage power grids ... In 1989') - with weaker (2-6) responses to version strings and long digit IDs, and one top example ('not only you but your family also') left unexplained.

Fires retrospectively on the leading token '1' (digit) or 'One'/' One' (number word), and rarely on fragments like ' del', exactly when it begins a multi-token number or number-led phrase that is part of a proper name or numbered identifier (highway/statute/model/film/street/honours titles such as Highway 136, section 1983, DC-10, One From the Heart). The same leading '1' as a bare count or ordinary calendar year (1 fish, year 1983, 1000 fish), and other leading digits in the same identifier slot (236, Two), stay near zero; gate activations show the '1' token is detected but the output is vetoed outside identifier contexts.

Retrospective detector for sustained neuroscience discourse (medial-temporal neuroanatomy such as perirhinal/hippocampal/parahippocampal/entorhinal, and clinical neurology such as rolandic epilepsy, meningioma case reports, DBS, neuroimaging): it fires on the generic token that follows the technical phrase (a conjunction, copula or preposition like and/was/with, adjacent punctuation, or a mid-word subword continuation), driven by the preceding term plus long-range clinical context and insensitive to the token after the peak; matched cardiology, legal, and everyday passages with the same structure do not activate it.

The positive pole fires on tokens that end inside a multi-byte UTF-8 character, i.e. the byte-level BPE fragments left where the tokenizer cut one character across two tokens (Japanese/Korean/Chinese/Greek pieces such as ' �' = a space plus the first two bytes of ギ/ヴ/メ, 'ー�', ' �'), which reach 2-5.7 while the token that finishes the same character stays near zero and complete words stay near zero. It is not a rare-token or non-Latin-script effect: bare continuation pieces that merely finish a character opened earlier behave like complete tokens (above-threshold rate 0.8% vs 4.9%, mean 0.16 vs 0.31), and the same word fires or falls silent depending only on whether the tokenizer split it; its large negative side is the separately verified standard-reproduced-text detector, so this is that neuron's weak, low-amplitude other end.

The negative pole fires on spans of standard, widely reproduced text: the recurring furniture of documents and web pages (licence/copyright and DRM/cookie notices, navigation and site statistics, citation/metadata tables, search- and formatting-help, HTML/JavaDoc templates) and well-known fixed passages such as prayers, pledges, famous openings and established encyclopedic leads. It stays near zero on prose that is being composed for the first time, including rewrites and newly invented passages in exactly the same genre: measured at 0.1-1.3 where the source passage it rewrites reaches 5.8-22, and it is silent on article prose, forum posts and code.

Fires on the introducer slot of a conventional frame that presents an act or stance of directed regard, attention, or evaluation — e.g. keep in __, keep/turned a __, caught/brought to my __, (have) expressed/drew __, came under __, took/receiving particular __, (it) is with __, also of __ — peaking on the frame's verb, preposition, possessive, or evaluative adjective. Swapping the complement noun (eye/ball, interest/anger, scrutiny/repair, attention/water) leaves the peak unchanged while swapping the introducing verb (caught->saw, expressed->stated, brought->walked, keep->walk) collapses it, so the trigger is the frame already read, not the upcoming word.
